name: Variables and Types
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: How Python stores values: binding, types, conversion, mutability, aliasing, equality and truthiness, compared with JavaScript.

lesson.intro: In Python a variable is a name attached to a value, and every value has a type that decides what you can do with it. This lesson builds the mental model behind every program you will write: what assignment really does, which values can change, when two names share one object, why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, and how all of it compares with JavaScript. Most confusing beginner bugs come from a gap in exactly this model.
objectives: Explain assignment as binding a name to an object and predict the effect of rebinding
Convert between str, int, float and bool and predict truncation, rounding and ValueError
Tell mutable from immutable types and avoid aliasing bugs with shallow and deep copies
Choose between == and is, and predict the truthiness of common values
Translate these ideas between Python and JavaScript, including where the languages differ

sections.title: Names point to values
sections.body:
A label maker is a better picture of Python variables than a filing cabinet. When you write `price = 5`, Python creates the int object 5 and ties the name `price` to it. A **variable** is a name bound to a value, not a box that holds one.

That picture explains assignment exactly:
- `x = 5` binds x to 5.
- `y = x` binds y to the same object x is bound to. Nothing is copied.
- `x = x + 1` computes a new value, 6, and moves the x label onto it. y is still bound to 5.

This is **binding**, and moving a name to a different value is **rebinding**. Rebinding one name never affects another name. (When the value itself can change, things get more interesting; that's the aliasing section.)

Python is **dynamically typed**: the type belongs to the value, not the name. The same name can refer to an int now and a string later, and `type(x)` tells you what x refers to right now. That flexibility is convenient, but a wrong assumption about a type only shows up when the line runs, which is why the sections on types and conversion matter.

A few assignment forms you'll use constantly:
- `a, b = 1, 2` assigns several names at once (tuple unpacking). The right side is fully evaluated first, so `a, b = b, a` swaps two values without a temporary variable.
- `count += 1` is shorthand for `count = count + 1`, and the same works for `-=`, `*=` and friends.
- `a = b = 0` binds both names to the same value.

Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, can't start with a digit, can't be a keyword such as `class` or `for`, and are case sensitive, so `total` and `Total` are different names. By convention Python uses `snake_case` for variables and functions, `UPPER_CASE` for constants you don't intend to change, and `CapWords` for classes. Pick names that say what the value means: `unpaid_invoices` beats `list2`.
sections.code:
x = 5
y = x            # y is bound to the same 5
x = x + 1        # x is rebound to a new value, 6
print(x, y)      # 6 5

x = "five"       # the name x can refer to any type
print(type(x))   # <class 'str'>

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a      # swap: the right side is evaluated first
print(a, b)      # 2 1

count = 0
count += 1
print(count)     # 1
sections.pitfall: Thinking `y = x` makes a copy. It binds a second name to the same object. With numbers and strings that never matters because they can't change, but with lists it causes the bugs in the aliasing section.

sections.title: Numbers: int, float and precision
sections.body:
Add ten cents and twenty cents in Python and you get `0.30000000000000004`. That's not a Python bug. It's how nearly every language stores decimals, and knowing why saves you from real bugs with money and comparisons.

Python has two main number types:
- `int` holds whole numbers with no size limit. `2 ** 100` is computed exactly, digit for digit, which is unusual: many languages cap integers at 64 bits.
- `float` holds numbers with a fractional part, stored in binary in 64 bits, which gives about 15 to 17 significant digits. `1e3` is the float `1000.0`.

Most decimal fractions, like 0.1, have no exact binary form, the same way 1/3 has no exact decimal form (0.3333...). The float stores the nearest binary value, and tiny errors appear when you combine them. So `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is False.

What to do about it:
- Compare floats with a tolerance: `math.isclose(a, b)`.
- For money, count whole cents as ints (`1999` instead of `19.99`), or use the `decimal` module and build values from strings: `Decimal("0.1")`.
- Round only for display, with an f-string such as `f"{total:.2f}"`, and keep full precision in calculations.

Mixing an int and a float gives a float, and `/` always gives a float. `//` and `%` give ints when both sides are ints.

One more surprise: `bool` is a kind of int. `True` behaves as 1 and `False` as 0 in arithmetic, so `True + True` is 2, and `sum()` of a list of True and False values counts the Trues. That's occasionally handy, but in most code keep bools for conditions.
sections.code:
import math
from decimal import Decimal

print(2 ** 100)            # 1267650600228229401496703205376
print(0.1 + 0.2)           # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)    # False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))       # True
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))   # 0.3

price_cents = 1999         # $19.99, stored exactly
print(f"${price_cents * 3 / 100:.2f}")   # $59.97

print(type(1e3), 1e3)      # <class 'float'> 1000.0
print(True + True)         # 2
sections.pitfall: Testing floats with `==`. A total built by adding prices may be 0.30000000000000004 rather than 0.3. Use `math.isclose()`, or keep money in integer cents.

sections.title: Converting between types
sections.body:
A CSV file gives you `"19.99"`, a form gives you `"42"` and a config file gives you `"False"`. All three are strings, and turning them into the values they describe is your job. Python won't guess.

Unlike JavaScript, Python never converts between text and numbers on its own: `"3" + 3` raises TypeError instead of quietly producing `"33"` or 6. You convert explicitly by calling the type you want, which is called **casting**:
- `int("42")` parses whole-number text. Surrounding spaces are fine (`int(" 42 ")` is 42), but `int("4.2")`, `int("")` and `int("forty")` raise ValueError.
- `float("19.99")` parses decimal text, and `float("3")` gives `3.0`.
- `str(10)` gives `"10"`, though an f-string such as `f"{n} items"` usually reads better.
- `int(-2.7)` drops the fractional part and gives -2. It **truncates toward zero**; it does not round. `math.floor(-2.7)` is -3, because flooring always rounds down.

`round()` has its own surprise: exact halves round to the nearest even number, which is called banker's rounding. `round(2.5)` is 2 and `round(3.5)` is 4. That avoids a bias when you round many values, but it catches people who expect 2.5 to become 3.

`bool()` uses truthiness (covered below), not the meaning of the text: `bool("False")` is True, because any non-empty string is truthy. To read a yes or no setting from text, compare the text: `flag = text.lower() == "true"`.

A good habit is to convert once, at the edge of your program where data comes in (keyboard, files, network), and work with proper types everywhere else. A number that is secretly a string causes bugs far away from where it entered.
sections.code:
print(int("42") + 1)       # 43
print(int(" 42 "))         # 42  (spaces are allowed)
print(float("19.99"))      # 19.99
print(str(10) + "0")       # 100
print(int(-2.7))           # -2  (truncates toward zero)
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))   # 2 4  (halves go to the even number)
print(bool("False"))       # True  (a non-empty string)

text = "False"
flag = text.lower() == "true"
print(flag)                # False
sections.pitfall: Using `bool()` to parse text. `bool("False")` and `bool("0")` are both True. Compare the text instead.

check.question: What does int(9.99) return?
check.explanation: int() truncates a float by dropping everything after the decimal point, so 9.99 becomes 9. Use round(9.99) if you want 10.

sections.title: Mutable and immutable values
sections.body:
You call `name.upper()` and name doesn't change, but you call `scores.append(70)` and scores does. The difference is whether the object can be changed after it's created.

**Mutable** objects can be changed in place. **Immutable** objects can't; any operation that seems to change one builds a new object instead.
- Immutable: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset and None.
- Mutable: list, dict and set, and most objects of classes you write yourself.

For immutable values, methods return the new value and leave the original alone, so you must keep the result: `name = name.upper()`. For mutable values, many methods change the object and return `None`: `append()`, `sort()`, `reverse()` and `extend()`. Writing `nums = nums.sort()` therefore replaces your list with None.

A **tuple** is the immutable cousin of a list: `point = (3, 4)`. You can read `point[0]`, but `point[0] = 5` raises TypeError. Tuples suit fixed groups of values, such as coordinates or a database row, and because they can't change they can be dictionary keys, which lists can't.

The `+=` operator shows the difference clearly. For a string, `s += "c"` builds a new string and rebinds s. For a list, `a += [2]` extends the existing list in place. If another name was bound to the same object, the string alias keeps the old value, but the list alias sees the change.

Why have immutable types at all? They are safe to share. If ten parts of a program refer to the same string, none of them can change it under the others. They also keep dictionaries reliable: a key whose value changed after it was stored could never be found again.
sections.code:
s = "hi"
s.upper()
print(s)              # hi   (the new string was thrown away)
s = s.upper()
print(s)              # HI

nums = [3, 1, 2]
result = nums.sort()
print(nums, result)   # [1, 2, 3] None

point = (3, 4)
print(point[0])       # 3
# point[0] = 5        # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

word = "ab"
alias = word
word += "c"
print(word, alias)    # abc ab
sections.pitfall: `nums = nums.sort()` or `nums = nums.append(4)` sets nums to None. In-place methods return None, so call them on their own line.

check.question: Which of these types is mutable?
check.explanation: Lists can be changed in place with append(), remove(), item assignment and so on. A tuple looks like a list but is immutable, like str and int.

sections.title: Aliasing and copies
sections.body:
A function is supposed to work out a discounted cart, and afterwards the original cart is discounted too. This is aliasing, and it's behind some of the most confusing bugs that beginners and professionals hit.

Assignment never copies. After `b = a`, both names refer to the same object. If that object is mutable, a change made through `b` is visible through `a`, because there is only one object. Two names for one object are **aliases**.

The same thing happens with function arguments. Passing a list into a function binds the parameter to the caller's list, so `items.append("x")` inside the function changes the caller's list. Sometimes that's what you want, but a function that quietly changes its input surprises the caller. Prefer returning a new value, or make it obvious from the function's name and docstring that it modifies its argument.

**Rebinding is not mutating.** `b = [9]` points b at a new list and leaves a untouched. Only operations that change the object itself (append, item assignment, `+=` on a list, sort) show through other names.

To get an independent list, copy it: `a.copy()`, `list(a)` or `a[:]`. These are **shallow copies**: a new outer list holding the same inner objects. If the items are themselves mutable, such as lists inside a list, the inner ones are still shared. `copy.deepcopy(a)` copies all the way down.

The same trap appears when building nested lists: `[[0] * 3] * 3` repeats one reference to a single inner list, so all three rows are the same row and changing one changes them all. Build each row separately, for example with `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`, a list comprehension covered in Intermediate Python.
sections.code:
import copy

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # an alias, not a copy
b.append(4)
print(a)           # [1, 2, 3, 4]

c = a.copy()       # a new list with the same items
c.append(5)
print(a, c)        # [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

board = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
shallow = board.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(board)
board[0][0] = 9
print(shallow)     # [[9, 0], [0, 0]]  (inner lists are shared)
print(deep)        # [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
sections.pitfall: Copying with `.copy()` and assuming nested lists are independent too. A shallow copy shares the inner lists; use `copy.deepcopy()` for nested data.

check.question: You run x = [0], then y = x, then y = [9]. What is x now?
check.explanation: y = [9] rebinds y to a brand-new list. Nothing happened to the list x refers to, so x is still [0]. Only mutating the shared list, for example y.append(9), would show up in x.

sections.title: Equality versus identity
sections.body:
Two students hand in identical essays. Are they the same essay? The content is equal, but there are two separate pieces of paper. Python makes the same distinction:
- `==` asks: do these two objects have equal values?
- `is` asks: are these the very same object?

Every object has an **identity**, shown by `id(x)`, which stays fixed for the object's lifetime. `a is b` is True exactly when `id(a) == id(b)`. Two lists built separately with the same items are `==` but not `is`. After `b = a`, they are both.

Use `is` for one main job: checking for `None`. `if result is None:` is the standard style. It's precise, because a class can redefine `==`, and it's different from `if not result:`, which is also true for 0, empty strings and empty lists.

Don't use `is` to compare numbers or strings. CPython reuses some small ints and short strings, so `is` can appear to work in a quick test and then fail with other values or in another context. Python even warns you (SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal) when you write something like `x is 5`. Use `==`.

`==` follows sensible rules across types. `1 == 1.0` is True because they are the same number, but `1 == "1"` is False: Python never turns text into a number to compare it. Membership tests use `==` too, so `[1, 2] in [[1, 2], [3]]` is True.

For your own classes, `==` falls back to identity unless you define an `__eq__` method, which the Object-Oriented Programming topic covers.
sections.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b)   # True False  (equal values, two objects)
print(a == c, a is c)   # True True   (one object, two names)
print(id(a) == id(c))   # True

result = None
print(result is None)            # True: the standard None check
print(1 == 1.0, 1 == "1")        # True False
print([1, 2] in [[1, 2], [3]])   # True: in uses ==
sections.pitfall: `if x == None` usually works, but `if x is None` is the correct idiom, and `if not x` is a different test that is also true for 0, "" and [].

check.question: Which comparison should you use to test whether a variable holds None?
check.explanation: None is a single object, so an identity check is exact and is the standard style. == None depends on the class's __eq__, not x is also true for 0 and empty values, and === is JavaScript, not Python.

sections.title: None and truthiness
sections.body:
A function looks up a discount code and returns nothing when the code is unknown, and three lines later `100 - discount` crashes. None and truthiness explain both the crash and the cleanest fixes.

`None` is Python's value for "nothing here". There is exactly one None object, of type `NoneType`. A function that ends without a `return` returns None, and so do in-place methods like `list.sort()`. Use None deliberately for "no value yet" or "not found", and test for it with `is None`.

Every value can be used as a condition. These are **falsy**, meaning they act like False in an `if` or `while`:
- `False`, `None`, `0` and `0.0`
- empty containers: `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `()` and `set()`

Everything else is **truthy**, including `"0"`, `"False"`, `" "` (a single space) and `[0]` (a list with one item). That's why `if items:` is the usual way to check that a list is not empty, and `if not name:` catches an empty string.

`and` and `or` don't just return True or False; they return one of their operands. `or` returns the first truthy operand, or the last one if none is truthy, so `name or "Guest"` gives a fallback when name is empty. `and` returns the first falsy operand, or the last one, so `user and user.name` only reads `.name` when there is a user.

Be careful when 0 or empty is a valid value. `quantity or 1` turns a real quantity of 0 into 1. When zero means something, test for None explicitly instead.
sections.code:
def greet():
    print("hi")

result = greet()        # prints hi
print(result)           # None
print(result is None)   # True

for value in [0, "", [], "0", [0], " "]:
    print(repr(value), bool(value))
# 0 False / '' False / [] False / '0' True / [0] True / ' ' True

name = ""
print(name or "Guest")  # Guest

quantity = 0
if quantity is None:    # 0 is a real answer here, so test for None
    quantity = 1
print(quantity)         # 0
sections.pitfall: Using `x or default` when x can legitimately be 0 or empty. The default silently replaces a valid value, so test `is None` instead.

sections.title: Python and JavaScript side by side
sections.body:
Most developers work in more than one language, and Python and JavaScript are the most common pair. The ideas in this lesson carry over directly, but several details differ, and those differences cause real bugs when you switch.

**Declaring names.** Python just assigns. JavaScript declares with `let` (can be rebound) or `const` (can't be rebound). `const` freezes the binding, not the value: `const nums = [1, 2]` still allows `nums.push(3)`. Avoid the old `var`.

**Numbers.** JavaScript has one `number` type, a 64-bit float like Python's float, so `7 / 2` is 3.5 in both and `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004 in both. There is no `//`; use `Math.floor(7 / 2)`. Whole numbers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1 (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`); beyond that JavaScript has a separate `bigint` type, written like `10n`.

**Nothing.** Python has `None`. JavaScript has two: `undefined` (never given a value) and `null` (deliberately empty). `typeof null` is `"object"`, a historical quirk.

**Equality.** JavaScript's `==` converts types before comparing (`0 == ""` is true), so always use `===`, which doesn't. For arrays and objects, `===` compares identity, like Python's `is`: `[1, 2] === [1, 2]` is false.

**Truthiness.** JavaScript's falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Empty arrays and empty objects are **truthy**, the opposite of Python. Check `arr.length === 0` instead of `!arr`.

**Conversion.** JavaScript converts implicitly where Python refuses: `"3" + 3` is `"33"` and `"3" * 3` is 9. Convert explicitly with `Number("3")` and `String(42)`.

**What stays the same:** strings are immutable, arrays and objects are mutable, and assignment creates aliases. Copy an array with `[...arr]` or `arr.slice()` (both shallow), and nested data with `structuredClone(obj)`.
sections.code:
let count = 0;
count += 1;               // let can be rebound
const nums = [1, 2];
nums.push(3);             // a const binding to a mutable array
console.log(nums);        // [1, 2, 3]

console.log(7 / 2, Math.floor(7 / 2));   // 3.5 3
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                  // 0.30000000000000004

console.log(0 == "", 0 === "");          // true false
console.log([1, 2] === [1, 2]);          // false (two different arrays)

console.log(Boolean([]), Boolean(""));   // true false
console.log("3" + 3, "3" * 3);           // 33 9
console.log(typeof 42, typeof 4.2);      // number number
sections.pitfall: Checking for an empty array with `if (!arr)` in JavaScript. Empty arrays are truthy there, so the check never fires. Use `arr.length === 0`.

check.question: In JavaScript you run const nums = [1, 2]; then nums.push(3);. What happens?
choices: nums stays [1, 2] because const arrays are frozen
push returns a new array and nums is unchanged
check.explanation: const stops you from rebinding the name (nums = [] would fail), but the array itself is mutable, so push changes it in place. Object.freeze() is what makes an array read-only.

keyTerms.definition: A name bound to a value. Assignment binds the name; it never copies the value.
Pointing a name at a different object. It never affects other names.
Types belong to values, not names, so one name can refer to values of different types over time.
Converting a value to another type explicitly, as in int("42") or str(42).
Tiny inaccuracies because most decimals, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form.
Can be changed in place after creation, like list, dict and set.
Can't be changed after creation, like int, str and tuple; operations return new objects.
Two or more names referring to the same object, so a mutation through one shows through all.
A new outer container holding the same inner objects, made by copy(), list() or [:].
Which object a name refers to, compared with is and shown by id().
Whether a value acts as True or False in a condition. None, 0 and empty containers are falsy in Python.
Python's single "no value" object, returned by functions that end without return.

summary: Variables are names bound to values; y = x binds a second name and never copies.
Ints are exact and unlimited, floats are approximate: compare with math.isclose() and keep money in cents.
Convert explicitly with int(), float() and str(); int() truncates toward zero and bool("False") is True.
Immutable values return new objects; mutable ones change in place, and their in-place methods return None.
== compares values and is compares identity: use is for None, and copy lists (deeply when nested) to avoid aliasing bugs.
None, 0 and empty containers are falsy in Python, but empty arrays and objects are truthy in JavaScript.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to someone new to programming why appending to list b also changed list a after b = a, why the same surprise can't happen with two names for one string, and how you would make b a real copy.

questions.question: Complete the line so it prints Count: 5
questions.explanation: + between a string and an int raises TypeError, so convert the int with str(count) first. int(count) is still an int, and ints have no .str() method. An f-string, f"Count: {count}", is another fix.

questions.question: What does this print?

questions.question: What does int(-3.8) return?

total must be declared as a float before the multiplication
questions.explanation: input() returns the string '9.99', and int() only parses whole-number text, so it raises ValueError rather than rounding. float(price) parses decimals.

questions.question: What is the difference between a mutable and an immutable object? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: A mutable object can be changed in place after it is created, such as a list with append(). An immutable object can't be changed; operations that seem to change it, such as str.upper(), return a new object instead.
questions.explanation: This difference decides whether aliasing can surprise you and whether you must save a method's result.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: b = a doesn't copy the list; both names refer to one list. Appending through b changes that list, so a also has 3 items.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append("x")

cart = []
add_item(cart)
add_item(cart)
print(cart)
questions.explanation: Passing cart to the function makes items an alias for the same list. Each call appends to that one list, so it ends with two items. The function doesn't need to return anything for the change to stick.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: == compares values, and both lists hold the same items, so it is True. is checks identity, and these are two separate list objects, so it is False.

scores.append(70)

questions.explanation: scores.copy() builds a new list with the same items. backup = scores would only create an alias, so backup would show 70 too. Lists have no clone() method, and [scores] is a new list whose single item is the original list.

questions.question: This should change only the top-left cell, but every row changes. Why?
choices: grid[0][0] refers to a whole column, not one cell
[0] * 3 creates a tuple, which can't be changed
The outer * 3 repeats a reference to one inner list; build rows with [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
Nested lists must be created with the list() function
questions.explanation: * on a list copies references, not the objects inside, so all three rows are one shared list and a change through grid[0] shows in every row. The comprehension creates a new inner list on each pass. [0] * 3 itself is fine, because ints are immutable.

questions.question: Which group contains only falsy values?
questions.explanation: Zero, the empty string, the empty list and None are all falsy. "0" and "False" are non-empty strings, and [0] is a list with one item, so all three are truthy.

questions.question: Why does this crash for the code HELLO?

questions.question: Which line prints the mathematically exact result?
questions.explanation: Ints have unlimited precision, so 2 ** 100 is exact. 0.1 + 0.7 prints 0.7999999999999999 and 1.1 * 3 prints 3.3000000000000003. Converting 2 ** 53 + 1 to a float loses the final 1, because floats can't represent every integer that large.

print(x, y)
questions.explanation: y = x binds y to the same 5. x = x + 1 creates a new value, 6, and rebinds only x. Rebinding one name never moves another.

questions.question: What does this print?

questions.question: Which of these are valid Python variable names? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Names can use letters, digits and underscores but can't start with a digit, so 2nd_place fails. total-price reads as total minus price, and class is a keyword. firstName is valid, though Python style prefers first_name.

questions.question: A settings file stores the text "True" or "False" in text. Which line turns it into the right bool in both cases?
questions.explanation: Comparing the text gives True only for "true" in any case. bool(text) is True for every non-empty string, including "False". int("True") raises ValueError, and a string is never the object True.

questions.question: Why does this raise TypeError?
choices: Tuples are immutable, so their items can't be reassigned; build a new tuple such as (5, point[1])
Tuple indexes start at 1, so point[0] doesn't exist
point must be created with tuple() before it can be indexed
A tuple can only hold strings
questions.explanation: Reading point[0] is fine, but assigning to it raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment. Create a new tuple, or use a list if the values need to change.

questions.question: What does this print?

t = s

a = [1]
b = a

print(t, b)
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so s += "c" builds a new string and rebinds s, leaving t as "ab". For a list, += extends the existing object in place, so b, an alias of a, sees [1, 2].

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
copied = original.copy()
copied[0].append(99)
copied.append([5])
print(original)
questions.explanation: copy() is shallow: the outer list is new, so appending [5] to copied doesn't touch original. The inner lists are shared, so appending 99 to copied[0] changes original[0] too.

questions.question: Complete the line so snapshot is unaffected by later changes to board.
questions.code:
import copy

board = [["X", ""], ["", "O"]]
snapshot = copy._____(board)
board[0][1] = "O"
print(snapshot[0])   # should still print ['X', '']
questions.explanation: deepcopy copies the inner lists too. copy.copy is a shallow copy, so the rows would still be shared and snapshot[0] would show ['X', 'O']. The copy module has no clone or shallow functions.

questions.question: Which check is True only when result is None, written the way Python style recommends?
questions.explanation: None is a single object, so is None is exact and idiomatic. == None relies on the object's __eq__, not result is also true for 0, "" and [], and === is JavaScript syntax.
